neighbours.label: A subject pronoun (he, she, they, it) that opens a new clause and takes up the person or thing just mentioned ('..., but he is out', '. She doesn't think'); the opposite pole fires on object ' it' after a verb
fire: My neighbour sold the bakery last spring. She now teaches evening classes in town.
The old captain rarely spoke of the war. He kept his medals in a drawer.
The twins look alike in every photo. They have never dressed the same, though.
Nobody expected the mayor to win again, but he is already planning a third term.
The engineers are tired of waiting. They want an answer before the weekend.
The word sounds harsh to visitors, but it is simply how people greet each other here.
Her grandmother grew up on the island. She still remembers the old ferry.
The players lost badly on Saturday, or at least, they failed to score at all.
quiet: My neighbour sold the bakery last spring and gave the keys to her.
The old captain kept the medals and rarely showed them to anyone.
The twins found the photo and hid it in a drawer.
Nobody expected the voters to choose him for a third term.
The engineers wrote an answer and sent it before the weekend.
The word sounds harsh, and visitors rarely use it when greeting people here.
Her grandmother kept the ferry tickets and showed them to us.
The coach blamed the players and made them train on Sunday.

notes: Card: peak tokens ' they', ' he', ' He', ' it', ' They', ' She', always the subject of a fresh clause after a comma, 'but' or a full stop; the - pole is 28/32 object ' it' ('Have it', 'got it'). Probes were weak: '. She opens' 0.29, 'yet he kept' 0.18, 'but they can' 0.17, 'but it is' 0.11; object pronouns 0.01-0.04. The contrast is clear but the level is near the 0.20 bar, so this may fail on the median.
